newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Corporate tax cuts seen key to Bonn tax deal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Corporate tax cuts seen key to Bonn tax deal.

text.p: Germany's ruling coalition and opposition Social Democrats (SPD) on Tuesday zeroed in on a possible deal to cut corporate taxes as the key to unlocking a compromise on broad reforms to battle record post-war unemployment.
But the day after rare face-to-face talks on sweeping tax reforms, both sides were cautious over whether they could meet the government's Easter deadline to agree big tax cuts.

An early agreement could promote investment and help put Germany's 4.7 million unemployed back to work, make tax collection more effective and strengthen Bonn's bid to lead Europe into economic and monetary union (EMU).
Failure would condemn the government's tax plans to lengthy wrangling in parliament -- where the SPD controls the upper house -- where they could drag on into the 1998 general election campaign.
Although big differences remain, SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine said he saw "no problem" with Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plan to cut the main corporate tax rate to 35 percent from 47.
But the opposition party stepped up its demands for cuts in Germany's job-killing labour costs that it wants to finance through an "ecological tax reform" -- jargon for raising petrol taxes.
"There will be no deal if nothing happens there," SPD parliamentary leader Rudolf Scharping said. Scharping will join a six-strong group which will hold more talks on Friday.
Coalition leaders said talks on corporate taxes and labour overheads could make progress, but warned that an SPD bid to boost consumer spending power could misfire.

"The SPD wants mainly to boost consumer demand, but we say that goes too far," Chancellery Minister Friedrich Bohl told German Radio. "But that would eventually disappear into thin air and fail to bring about the structural changes we urgently need to boost our competitiveness."
Agreement on corporate tax cuts would mark a first step towards a wider agreement over Waigel's plans to cut 30 billion marks ($18 billion) in taxes over the next two years.

Although the two sides broadly agree on cutting the bottom rate of income tax, they are far apart over how to tax high earners. Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition wants a drop in the top rate to 39 percent from 53 percent.

Scharping said the SPD was not completely opposed to a top-rate tax cut. But, he added, that must not be financed by raising value-added-tax or abolishing tax relief on pay for night, weekend and holiday work.
The coalition argues that the constitutional court in Karlsruhe could intervene if corporate and top-rate income taxes are too far apart.
The SPD rejects that argument and received strong backing on Tuesday from Germany's two most powerful trade unions.
